label: bm-4d-printing-review
topic: 4D printing and shape-morphing: state of the art with numbers
summary: Survey of 4D-printed shape-morphing classes with numbers read from fetched full texts (Europe PMC / NCBI PMC / publisher pages), plus checks of earlier agent files. Headline results. (1) CONTRADICTION of spec-hygromorph-4d: a humidity-actuated vat-photopolymer part does exist. Goodarzi Hosseinabadi et al. (Small 2024, DOI 10.1002/smll.202306387) printed a PEG-polyurethane diacrylate ink by SLA (400 nm) and custom DLP (380 nm); thin films fold reversibly in humid air in under 1 s, a 50 um film folds over 5x faster than a 150 um film, and a 0.1 mm film lifts 50 mg (5x its own weight) at RH about 90 percent. It is a high-swelling (about 600 percent in water) hydrogel-like ink, not a Formlabs resin, with no curvature numbers and no Timoshenko analysis, so the 'no SLA/DLP humidity actuator' gap is closed but the 'Formlabs-resin hygromorph with a Timoshenko check' gap stays open. (2) CONTRADICTION/REFINEMENT of the '<1 percent in 24 h' statement: it is true for Formlabs' 1 cm cube table (Elastic 50A V2 water 0.7 percent, Rigid 10K <0.1 percent; the 39.2 percent IPA figure for Elastic 50A V2 vs <0.1 percent for Rigid 10K is CONFIRMED) but Flexible 80A Resin V2's own datasheet (ASTM D471 slab) gives +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume after 1 day in deionized water (+9 and +7 percent at 1 week), and a Formlabs Dental LT Clear V2 part gained 29.53 ug/mm3 of water in a week in a third-party study (about 2.7 percent by mass if density is 1.1 g/cm3, my assumption). The number depends on the test method, specimen thickness and duration. (3) Class numbers: thermal SMPs/LCEs respond in tens of seconds to minutes with large strains (LCE 80 percent programmed strain, 11 cycles; SMP bilayer about 20 s) but need heat; swelling hydrogels are slow (diffusion) and weak (forces under 1 N, about 2 kPa blocking stress vs 100-350 kPa for muscle), though thin films can be fast; cellulose-filled FFF bilayers reach 0.0155 mm^-1 in 30 min over 170 cycles (Cheng 2024); wood bilayers take 24 h at 4-8 mm and about 400 h at 15-30 mm. (4) Timoshenko: published comparisons exist for wood, paper, FFF filaments and, newly, a 2026 FFF polyamide bilayer (predicted 36.4 vs measured 35.3 +/- 3.1 deg, n=3, arXiv 2604.26367); none found for vat-photopolymer or SLS parts. I re-ran the project's ceiling numerically (max f = 1.5000 on a 401x401 log grid) and applied it to a new vat-printed GelMA bilayer: ceiling radius 10.9 mm against a tightest measured 11 mm (plausibility only; figure data unreadable). (5) Formal verification: no hygromorph or bilayer design with a proof-assistant-checked law was found (0 hits in Europe PMC and arXiv searches). The nearest item, arXiv 2604.26367, calls its pipeline 'verified' in a category-theory sense and its full text has no Lean/Coq/Isabelle mention. Searches were limited to Europe PMC, arXiv, Crossref and publisher pages, so absence is probable, not proven.
lay_summary: Some printed objects change shape on their own after they are made, for example a flat strip that curls when the air gets damp. I checked the numbers for the main families: heat-triggered plastics, water-swelling gels, wood-fibre plastics and two-layer strips. Heat-triggered plastics move in seconds to minutes but need a heat source; gels and wood respond to humidity alone but are slow and weak, like a wet sponge compared with a muscle. The earlier team notes said nobody had made a humidity-driven part in a light-cured resin printer, but a 2024 paper did, using a special gel-like ink that folds a thin film in under a second when it senses moisture. Formlabs' own tables say their ordinary resins soak up under 1 percent water in a day, which holds for small cubes, but one soft resin gains 8 percent weight in a day on a different test, so the true figure depends on how you test it. I found no published design that was restricted by a computer-checked mathematical proof, which is the gap this project can fill.

findings.claim: SMP 4D printing (multimaterial, PolyJet-type photopolymer jetting): SMPs are stiffer and faster than hydrogels, response in seconds to minutes depending on actuation temperature.
findings.value: response = seconds to minutes; E = MPa to GPa
findings.evidence_quote: faster response rates (in the scale of seconds to minutes depending on actuation temperature)

findings.claim: Tunable methacrylate SMP networks span rubbery modulus up to about 100 MPa, glass transition about -50 to 180 C and failure strain up to about 300 percent (Ge 2016).
findings.value: E_rubbery=~MPa-~100 MPa; Tg=-50..180 C; failure strain<=~300%
findings.evidence_quote: rubbery modulus (from ∼MPa to ∼100 MPa), glass transition temperature (from ∼−50 °C to ∼180 °C), and the failure strain (up to ∼300%)

findings.claim: Direct-4D-printed SMP/elastomer bilayer (Ding 2017): glassy SMP about 1 GPa laminated to elastomer about 1 MPa; samples complete the shape change in about 20 s in hot water; this is a programmed bilayer (curvature set by built-in compressive strain), one-way but reprogrammable.
findings.value: E_SMP=~1 GPa; E_elastomer=~1 MPa; t=~20 s at 62 C; layer 30 um; bilayer 60x5x(0.3-1.2) mm
findings.evidence_quote: At room temperature, the SMP is glassy with a modulus of ~1 GPa, which is two to three orders of magnitude stiffer than the elastomer ( E ~ 1 MPa)

findings.claim: Ding 2017 timing: the bilayers finished transforming about 20 s after immersion at the set temperature.
findings.evidence_quote: After ~20 s, the samples had completed the transformation

findings.claim: Review-level SMP recovery times: about 35 s (magnetic), 75 s (electric current), 160 s (light) for printed SMP composites. Secondary source, not re-checked against the primary papers.
findings.evidence_quote: The printed snowflake model demonstrated rapid shape recovery from a temporary form to the original shape within 35 s under a magnetic field.

findings.claim: Vat-photopolymer (DLP, 405 nm) two-stage LCE (Jiang 2026): programmed at 80 percent strain, reversible actuation strain close to that target for the best formulations, 11 cycles without degradation, saturation after more than 30 min at 80 C (DMA, 1 C/min). Thermal stimulus, not humidity.
findings.value: programming strain=80%; cycles shown=11; saturation >30 min at 80 C
findings.evidence_quote: AE_3–AE_18 samples achieved actuation strains close to the target programming strain.

findings.claim: Same LCE paper: sample AE_18 repeated 11 consecutive cycles without noticeable degradation.
findings.evidence_quote: AE_18 was subjected to 11 consecutive cycles and exhibited consistent strain evolution without noticeable degradation

findings.claim: Review table of printed LCE filaments (representative literature values): actuation strain 28 to 110 percent, stress 0.15 to 0.55 MPa, cycles to 50 percent decay 100 to more than 1000. Secondary table whose references were not checked.
Hydrogel actuators are slow because they rely on diffusion of water (review, Chau and Amstad 2026).
findings.evidence_quote: Untethered soft actuators typically are slow because they rely on the diffusion of water.

findings.claim: Hydrogel actuator force: swelling and contraction forces for most hydrogel actuators are below 1 N, although the osmotic pressure can reach megapascals.
findings.evidence_quote: the swelling and contraction forces for most hydrogel actuators are less than 1 N

findings.claim: Table in the same review: typical hydrogel actuators give about 2 kPa actuation (blocking) stress against 100 to 350 kPa for mammalian skeletal muscle; toughness 1-10 kJ/m3 for typical hydrogels.
findings.value: sigma_block=2 kPa (hydrogel) vs 100-350 kPa (muscle); toughness=1-10 kJ/m3
findings.evidence_quote: Actuation stress ( i.e. blocking stress) 2 kPa — 100–350 kPa

findings.claim: Vat-photopolymerised GelMA (Guida 2026): per-layer exposure time sets crosslink density and therefore swelling: 30 s exposure gives the highest linear swelling, 7.7 percent, 70 s only 1 percent (24 h, DMEM, 37 C).
findings.value: LS=7.7% (30 s) vs 1% (70 s) at 24 h; E_swollen=14.5-20.2 kPa
findings.evidence_quote: the sample printed with a 30 s exposure exhibited the highest swelling ratio at 7.7%, whereas the sample printed with a 70 s exposure showed only 1% linear expansion

findings.claim: Guida 2026 bilayers (20 x 2 x 1 mm, 65 s lower layer and 35 s upper layer, thickness split varied in 100 um steps) bent to radii of curvature of 11 to 20 mm after 24 h in culture medium; Figure 5a with the per-geometry values could not be read.
findings.evidence_quote: enabling controlled bending of the printed structures upon immersion in aqueous media, with radii of curvature between 11 and 20 mm depending on the geometry.

findings.claim: Guida 2026 modelled the bilayer by finite elements using a thermal-expansion analogy (swelling strain entered as expansion coefficient); the paper does not use or cite Timoshenko's formula (0 occurrences of 'Timoshenko' in the full text).
findings.evidence_quote: Swelling-induced deformation was simulated through thermal expansion, by assigning the experimentally determined linear swelling ratios as the materials’ coefficients of thermal expansion.

findings.claim: Guida 2026 table of swollen GelMA after 24 h, by exposure time: E (kPa) and linear swelling LS (percent): 30 s 14.48 / 7.83; 40 s 15.30 / 7.11; 50 s 17.07 / 5.52; 60 s 18.64 / 2.02; 70 s 20.23 / 0.70.

Anisotropic-fibre patterned hydrogel (Gladman 2016): composite hydrogel with cellulose-fibril alignment along printed paths, shape change on immersion in water. Swelling strains, curvatures and times are in the paywalled full text and were NOT read.
findings.evidence_quote: we printed composite hydrogel architectures that are encoded with localized, anisotropic swelling behaviour controlled by the alignment of cellulose fibrils along prescribed four-dimensional printing pathways.

findings.claim: A humidity-driven vat-photopolymer actuator DOES exist in the literature: Goodarzi Hosseinabadi et al. (Small 2024) printed a PEG-polyurethane diacrylate ink by SLA (400 nm, 2 mW/cm2) and by a custom DLP printer (380 nm, 700 mW/cm2); films fold in humid air. This contradicts spec-hygromorph-4d, which listed 'any SLA/DLP bilayer actuated by ambient relative humidity' as not found.
findings.value: printer: SLA 400 nm 2 mW/cm2; custom DLP 380 nm 700 mW/cm2
findings.evidence_quote: a custom-built DLP printer which allowed ink printing at a very high intensity light (700 mW/cm 2 at 380 nm wavelength)

findings.claim: Small 2024 film response to skin humidity: folds in under 1 s, reversibly, 'apparently unlimited' cycles claimed (not counted).
findings.evidence_quote: Like a cantilever beam, the film rapidly initiated folding in less than 1s.

findings.claim: Small 2024 thickness scaling: a 50 um film folded over 5 times faster than a film of about 150 um (3x thinner gives over 5x faster, i.e. between linear (3x) and diffusive quadratic (9x) scaling; the authors fitted no exponent).
findings.evidence_quote: A film having 50 μm thickness folded over 5 times faster compared to a film of around 150 μm thickness

findings.claim: Small 2024 force: a 6 x 18 x 0.1 mm film carried about 50 mg (5 times its own weight) in humid air at RH about 90 percent.
findings.value: load=50 mg (5x film weight); film 6x18x0.1 mm; RH~90%
findings.evidence_quote: The gripper could load an object (about 50 mg, 5 times the film weight)

findings.claim: Small 2024 material: the PEG-PU network swells to a degree of about 600 percent in water, far beyond any stock Formlabs resin; swelling falls with longer exposure per layer. It is not a Formlabs resin, and no curvature numbers or Timoshenko analysis were found in the text.
findings.evidence_quote: swollen in MilliQ water with a swelling degree of approximately 600%

findings.claim: Cellulose-filled FFF bilayers (Cheng 2024, livMatS): full transformation between 30 and 90 percent RH within 30 min.
findings.evidence_quote: The bilayers reach a full transformation between two RH extremes of 30% and 90% within 30 minutes

findings.claim: Cheng 2024: at 80 percent RH all bilayers had mean curvature 0.0155 mm^-1 (radius 64.5 mm, own arithmetic 1/0.0155).
findings.evidence_quote: At 80% RH, all bilayers are observed with an average curvature of 0.0155 mm −1

findings.claim: Cheng 2024 reversibility: 170 humidity cycles, consistent curvature at 30 percent RH.
findings.evidence_quote: For all 170 tested actuation cycles, the bilayers display consistent curvatures at the low RH of 30%.

findings.claim: Cheng 2024 does not use Timoshenko's formula anywhere in its text (0 occurrences); Tahouni 2023 mentions the modified Timoshenko model only as future work (1 occurrence).
findings.evidence_quote: the modified Timoshenko model 5 , 38 can be utilized to explore other bilayer layups

findings.claim: Wood bilayers (Rueggeberg and Burgert 2015): moisture content falls from about 18 to about 10 percent in 24 h; confirms earlier agent.
findings.evidence_quote: A decrease of the wood moisture content from around 18% to around 10% within 24 hours was observed

findings.claim: Same paper: curvature up to 8.7e-3 mm^-1 for passive spruce up to 1 mm, and 1.5e-3 mm^-1 for 4 mm spruce after 24 h.
findings.evidence_quote: curvatures up to 8.7*10 -3 mm -1 were reached, whereas bilayers with a spruce layer of 4mm thickness reached a curvature of 1.5*10 -3 mm -1 after 24 hours only.

findings.claim: Thick mass-timber bilayers (Groenquist 2019, 15-45 mm): moisture equilibrates after about 400 h; the 45 mm series had not equilibrated after 900 h. Across this and the other wood/FFF sources the response time climbs steeply with thickness (30 min sub-mm FFF, 24 h at 4-8 mm, about 400 h at 15-30 mm); no exponent is claimed because materials and end-point criteria differ.
findings.evidence_quote: WMCs were approximately equilibrated after 400 hours in the dry target climate, except for the bilayer series with a thickness of 45 mm, for which an equilibration is not visible after 900 hours.

findings.claim: Material-jetting bilayers (Raviv 2014, Stratasys): hydrophilic UV-curable polymer absorbs water to up to 200 percent of its original volume.
findings.evidence_quote: creates a hydrogel with up to 200% of the original volume

findings.claim: Fused-filament bilayers have a published Timoshenko comparison: Krueger 2021 adapts Timoshenko's model for unequal effective widths and validates it on a 4D-printed bilayer system.
findings.value: published Timoshenko comparison exists for FFF
findings.evidence_quote: Timoshenko’s model [ 23 ] is adapted to account for unequal effective widths of the active and passive layer.

findings.claim: A 2026 FFF hygromorph with Timoshenko-based prediction (Marom, Tibbits, Zardini, Buehler, arXiv 2604.26367): PA6-GF active / PA612-CF passive bilayer; baseline hygroscopic bending predicted 36.4 deg vs measured 35.3 +/- 3.1 deg (3.0 percent error, n=3); all four cases within one standard deviation.
findings.evidence_quote: All four predictions agree with the measured mean to within one standard deviation.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED: Formlabs solvent page 24 h 1 cm cube: Elastic 50A Resin V2 takes up 39.2 percent isopropyl alcohol; Rigid 10K under 0.1 percent; water 0.7 percent for Elastic 50A V2 and under 0.1 percent for Rigid 10K. Columns: IPA is the 10th data column, water the 18th.
Same page, Rigid 10K row.

CONTRADICTION (method-dependent): the claim 'stock Formlabs resins gain under 1 percent in 24 h in water' holds on the 1 cm cube table but NOT for Flexible 80A Resin V2 on its datasheet: ASTM D471 slab, deionized water, 1 day: +8 percent mass, +3 percent volume, -26 Shore A points; 1 week: +9 percent mass, +7 percent volume. I read the page as an image to resolve a garbled text layer. The older Flexible 80A (V1) cube row gives 0.7 percent.
findings.value: water 1 day: dm=+8%, dV=+3%, dHardness=-26; 1 week: +9%, +7%, -27

findings.claim: Flexible 80A V2 1-week row.

Flexible 80A Resin (V1) cube row on the solvent page: water 0.7 percent, IPA 11.7 percent. So the 'under 1 percent' statement of the earlier agent is true for V1 and for the cube method, not for V2 under D471.

Flexible 80A V2 mass gain (8 percent) exceeds what the volume gain (3 percent) allows for water (water volume would be about 8 x 1.09 = 8.7 percent of the part volume by my arithmetic using the TDS density 1.09 g/cm3 from the earlier agent file), so the two numbers are not mutually consistent as swelling; extraction, porosity or the wipe-dry step may play a role. Flagged, not resolved.

Third-party measurement on a Formlabs resin: Dental LT Clear V2 printed on a Form 3B+ (low force stereolithography) took up 29.53 ug/mm3 of water in one week, the highest of the printed aligner resins tested.
findings.evidence_quote: Dental LT Clear V2 displayed the highest sorption (mean 29.53 µg/mm³)

findings.claim: Same study confirms the printer and resin: 'Dental LT Clear V2 (LT) (Formlabs Inc., Somerville, MA, USA) Form 3B+'.
findings.evidence_quote: Dental LT Clear V2 (LT) (Formlabs Inc., Somerville, MA, USA) Form 3B+ (Formlabs Inc., Somerville, MA, USA) Low force stereolithography (LFS)

findings.claim: My conversion: 29.53 ug/mm3 = 29.53 mg/cm3 = 0.02953 g water per cm3; if the resin density were 1.1 g/cm3 (assumed, not stated in the source) that is about 2.7 percent by mass, and an upper bound of about 1.0 percent isotropic linear strain if water volume simply adds (1.02953^(1/3)-1). So a Formlabs-printed resin takes up about 3 percent water in a week, three to four times the 24 h cube figures for the stock resins, consistent with the earlier agent's Grey V5 week figure (3.2 percent).

Own check of the project's ceiling: a log-grid scan of f(m,n)=6(1+m)^2/[3(1+m)^2+(1+mn)(m^2+1/(mn))] over m,n in 0.01-100 never exceeded 1.5 (maximum 1.5000000000000002 on the grid) and equals 1.5 at m^2 n = 1 for m = 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5; f is symmetric under swapping the layers (f(2,0.4) = f(0.5,2.5) = 1.4815). This is a numerical sanity check; the proof is the Lean file in the project record.

Own test of the ceiling on a new vat-printed bilayer (Guida 2026): from the table, delta-epsilon between the 35 s layer (mean of 30 s and 40 s rows: 7.47 percent) and the 65 s layer (mean of 60 s and 70 s rows: 1.36 percent, my assumption) is 6.11 percent; with h = 1 mm the ceiling gives a smallest possible radius R = h/(1.5 d_eps) = 10.9 mm. The paper's tightest measured radius is 11 mm. With moduli 14.89 and 19.44 kPa (n = 1.305) Timoshenko predicts R = 11.0 mm at a 1:1 split and 11.0-12.3 mm for 40-70 percent active layer, 19.2 mm at 20 percent, 36 mm at 10 percent. Consistent with the 11-20 mm range, but the per-geometry data (Figure 5a) could not be read, so this is a plausibility check, not a validation.
findings.value: R_min,ceiling=10.9 mm vs measured 11 mm; sweep R=11.0-36 mm

findings.claim: Own energy-density bounds (0.5*E*d_eps^2, fully blocked uniform layer; an upper bound, not a measurement): GelMA swollen 14.9 kPa at 6.1 percent = 28 J/m3; beech E=0.65 GPa at d_eps 2.5 percent = 203 kJ/m3; PA12-like E=1.5 GPa at 0.35 percent (earlier agent's estimate) = 9.2 kJ/m3. Printed LCE filament sigma x strain = 88-165 kJ/m3 from the review table (upper bound). So moisture-driven polymer actuators span roughly four decades in work density, wood and LCE high, hydrogels lowest.

key_claims.claim: A vat-photopolymer (SLA/DLP) humidity-actuated 4D part has been published (Small 2024, PEG-polyurethane ink, film folds in under 1 s, 50 um film over 5x faster than 150 um, lifts 50 mg), contradicting the earlier 'none found' gap; it is not a Formlabs resin and has no Timoshenko analysis.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Like a cantilever beam, the film rapidly initiated folding in less than 1s.

key_claims.claim: The 'stock Formlabs resins gain under 1 percent in 24 h in water' statement is method-dependent: Flexible 80A Resin V2 gains +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume in 1 day in water on its datasheet (ASTM D471 slab). The Elastic 50A V2 39.2 percent IPA vs Rigid 10K under 0.1 percent figure is confirmed.

No hygromorph or bilayer design constrained by a proof-assistant-checked law was found; the closest (arXiv 2604.26367) is 'verified' only in a category-theoretic sense, uses the Timoshenko formula on an FFF polyamide bilayer (36.4 vs 35.3 +/- 3.1 deg), and never mentions Lean, Coq or Isabelle.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Here we present a category theoretic compositional framework for verified nature-derived design.

key_claims.claim: Humidity-driven polymer actuators are slow and weak compared with thermal SMPs/LCEs: hydrogel forces are under 1 N, cellulose-filled FFF bilayers need 30 min for full transformation, thin wood 24 h, thick timber about 400 h.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The bilayers reach a full transformation between two RH extremes of 30% and 90% within 30 minutes

recommendations: Treat Goodarzi Hosseinabadi 2024 (Small, DOI 10.1002/smll.202306387) as prior art for 'humidity-driven vat-photopolymer film'. The defensible novelty is narrower: a Formlabs-printable resin pair (Form 4 SLA) and/or an SLS powder pair, with a design ceiling proven in Lean and a curvature-vs-Timoshenko comparison, which no source found has.

Measure, do not assume, the swelling of the candidate Formlabs resins: Flexible 80A V2 as an ASTM D471-type slab and as thin (0.2-0.5 mm) strips, in humid air at 30/60/90 % RH, with linear strain from digital images, because the datasheet (+8 % mass, +3 % volume) and cube table (0.7 % for V1) disagree and thickness changes everything.

Benchmark the proof of concept against the numbers here: 0.0155 mm^-1 and 30 min and 170 cycles (Cheng 2024); sub-1 s folding of 50-100 um films and 50 mg lifted (Small 2024); radius 11 mm and 24 h immersion (Guida 2026). Report cycles survived and a blocking force or moment, which most papers omit.

For the Timoshenko comparison, request or digitise Figure 5a of Guida 2026 (curvature vs layer-thickness split) and test the 3/2 ceiling on it; my calculation gives a ceiling radius of 10.9 mm against a tightest measured 11 mm, which is a prediction worth confirming with the real per-geometry data.

Cite Marom, Tibbits, Zardini, Buehler (arXiv 2604.26367) as the nearest 'verified' hygromorph pipeline and state plainly that its verification is categorical, not kernel-checked; the project's Lean ceiling theorem is a different, machine-checked kind of constraint. Check whether the preprint has since been peer reviewed before quoting it.

Retire the sentence 'every current Formlabs SLA resin gains under 1 percent in water in 24 h' from project documents or add 'on the 1 cm cube test'; use the D471 figure for Flexible 80A V2 and the third-party one-week figure for Dental LT Clear V2.

Have a library-access agent pull the paywalled numbers (Gladman 2016 swelling strains and curvature; Kotikian 2018 (10.1002/adma.201706164, seen in a Europe PMC listing, not opened) and other primary LCE papers for force and work density) before the paper quotes class-level force or work density; I could only give review-level and own upper-bound figures.

glossary.plain: 3D printing an object that then changes shape over time in response to heat, water or another trigger.
A plastic that can be fixed in one shape and springs back to another when warmed.
A rubbery plastic whose molecules line up, so it shrinks or stretches strongly when heated.
A soft, water-swollen gel such as jelly or a contact lens.
A material that bends or twists as it takes up or loses moisture from the air, like a pine cone scale.
Two bonded layers where one expands more than the other, so the strip curls.
A 1925 equation that predicts how much a two-layer strip curls from the layers' thicknesses, stiffnesses and the difference in how much each swells.
The project's proven limit: the strip's curvature times its thickness can never exceed 1.5 times the swelling difference.
Printing by shining light into a tank of liquid resin so that it hardens layer by layer.
Printing by melting layers of plastic powder with a laser.
Printing by squeezing melted plastic filament through a nozzle.
How damp the air is, as a percentage of the most water it can hold.
How sharply something bends; 0.0155 per millimetre means it bends like a circle 64.5 mm in radius.
How much useful work a material can do per unit of its volume, for example per cubic metre.
Slow spreading of water through a material; thicker parts take much longer.
Rubbing alcohol, used to wash printed resin parts.
A proof program that checks every step of a mathematical argument so a human cannot slip an error past it.
A standard soak test measuring how much a rubber gains in weight and volume in a liquid.
